title: Should Swarajya stay on the spam blacklist? — the doxxing fight
context: Full section kept: 15 comments, 6 voices, three roots plus a late procedural note, 3–5 Nov 2026. The thread slides from ‘should we re-evaluate?’ into a doxxing-attribution fight that ends in an explicit concession. Levels span 0–7; the tu quoque at move 8 is the underhanded pivot.

claims.text: The blacklisting discussion was well-attended and rested on more than editors’ partisanship.
claims.span: There was more that this decision was predicated on than the partisanship of its editors

claims.text: The absence of reports about a source’s misinformation does not mean it does not publish misinformation.
claims.span: The absence of reports about its misinformation do not mean that it does not publish misinformation

claims.text: Changed facts justify reevaluating the blacklist entry.
Little new damning evidence against Swarajya has emerged in the last 3–4 years.
claims.span: in last 3-4 years, there hasn't been much damning evidence against it

claims.text: Swarajya was blacklisted for doxing a Wikipedia editor who diverged from its politics; the editor was harassed off-wiki and stopped editing.
claims.span: Swarajya was placed on the spam blacklist because it doxed a Wikipedia editor who diverged from the publication's political perspective

claims.text: Swarajya should remain on the spam blacklist.
claims.span: and should remain on the spam blacklist

weak_points.note: The case for reevaluation never names what changed — ‘many facts have changed’ carries no content, so the conclusion rests entirely on the absence-of-new-evidence premise its own author concedes proves little.
An argument from absence. Reconrabbit’s matching request for evidence of misinformation is never answered by anyone — the misinformation half of the case is asserted on both sides without exhibits.

The tu quoque is never connected to any premise and never answered: it insinuates the victim’s own bans mitigate the doxing, which no one states or contests. The referent of ‘they’ is itself ambiguous.
The ‘technically not reliability’ distinction is never cashed out — which reliability criterion does doxxing fail? The practice-over-principle gap stays undefined.
The retreat is never made precise: referenced via what — name, family name, identifiable details? The archive check answers it, but the concession arrives before the distinction is stated.
Asserted without a mechanism — who would report misinformation, to whom? It is conceded by the other side, which may be why it is never examined.
